title: Introduction to Linear Regression

segments.title: Introduction to Linear Regression
segments.objective: Introduce the concept of modeling relationships between two variables using a straight line.
segments.narration: Welcome! Today we are exploring linear regression, a powerful tool in statistics that lets us model the relationship between two variables. Imagine you want to know how study hours affect test scores. By plotting our data points on a graph, we can see a clear upward trend. Linear regression finds the best-fitting straight line through these points, allowing us to understand the trend and make future predictions with confidence.

elements.text: Linear regression helps us model the relationship between an independent variable (x) and a dependent variable (y) using a straight line.

quiz.prompt: What is the main purpose of linear regression in statistics?
choices: To model the relationship between two variables using a straight line
To calculate the exact exact average without any error
To measure categorical variables like eye color
To prove that studying has no effect on scores

segments.title: The Regression Equation: y = 45 + 6x
segments.objective: Break down the y-intercept and slope using the study hours and test scores example.
segments.narration: Let's examine the heart of linear regression: the straight line equation, y equals 45 plus 6x. Here, y represents the predicted test score, and x is the number of study hours. The number 45 is our y-intercept. This means if a student studies for zero hours, our model predicts a baseline test score of 45. The number 6 is the slope. For every additional hour a student spends studying, their predicted test score increases by 6 points. Let us visualize this on our graph with a solid line starting at 45 and rising steadily upward as study hours increase.

elements.text:
Intercept (45): Base score with 0 study hours.
Slope (6): Score increase per study hour.
elements.caption: Interpreting Parameters

quiz.prompt: Using the equation y = 45 + 6x, what is the predicted test score for a student who studies for 3 hours?

segments.title: Making Predictions and Understanding Residuals
segments.objective: Predict a test score for 3 study hours and explain what residuals represent.
segments.narration: Now that we have our equation, y equals 45 plus 6x, let us use it to make a prediction. Suppose a student studies for 3 hours. We substitute x equals 3 into our equation: 45 plus 6 times 3 gives us 45 plus 18, which equals 63. Our model predicts a test score of 63! However, real-world data is rarely perfect. If that same student actually scores a 70, the difference between the actual score and our predicted score is called a residual. Here, the residual is 70 minus 63, which equals positive 7. This positive residual means our model underestimated the student's actual performance. Residuals help us measure how well our line fits the actual data points.

elements.text:
Residual = Actual - Predicted
Residual = 70 - 63 = +7

A positive residual means the actual score was higher than the model predicted.
elements.caption: Understanding Residuals

Here is a real-world example of slope: imagine you are driving a car and your speed is 60 miles per hour. For every 1 hour that passes, the distance you travel increases by 60 miles. In that relationship, the slope is 60! It tells us the constant rate of change.
What does the slope of six mean in this example? Explain in two short sentences.
The slope of 6 means that for every additional hour spent studying, a student's predicted test score increases by 6 points. It represents the constant rate of change in our linear model.
